00. Course overview

Yale University — Death (PHIL 176) · English notes for all 26 lectures

Instructor: Shelly Kagan (Clark Professor of Philosophy, Yale University) · recorded Autumn 2007 · Open Yale Courses · roughly 41–52 minutes per lecture.

The question this course asks is not the factual one — what happens after death — but a chain of philosophical ones: What is a person? What is death? Why, if at all, is death bad? Is fear of death rational? Given that you must die, how should you live? Under what conditions can suicide be rational, or even morally permissible?

Kagan works in the analytic style: first cut the concepts clean (soul / body / person; death vs. dying vs. being dead), then lay out the best argument for each position in turn and look for the flaw. His own leanings are physicalism plus the deprivation account, but the course deliberately withholds a verdict. What it actually delivers is not a set of answers but the ability to tell a good argument from a bad one.

The six modules

1. What is a person (02–06) Dualism vs. physicalism. The soul can be neither observed nor introspected, so the only live defence is inference to the best explanation: find a feature F that physicalism cannot explain and that positing a soul explains better. The candidates are tried in turn — being alive, purposive motion, free will, belief and desire, emotion.

2. Plato's arguments for immortality (07–09) The arguments of the Phaedo: from the soul's bringing life and admitting no death, to the claim that only composites can be destroyed and the soul is simple. Each is tested and each is found wanting.

3. Personal identity (10–13) What keeps you the same person over time? The soul theory, the body theory and the personality (psychological continuity) theory each face fatal counterexamples — fission cases, hypnosis, amnesia, radical character change. The module ends in a turn: perhaps identity itself is not what matters, but survival, continuation, psychological connectedness.

4. The nature of death and believing you will die (14–15) Death is not a state but a terminus; imagining "my death" as something I undergo is a trick of the imagination. The key distinction is death vs. dying vs. being dead.

5. The badness of death (16–21) If death is the end, what is bad about it? The deprivation account: death is bad because it deprives you of goods you would otherwise have had — so dying young is worse than dying old, and immortality may not be good at all (repetition, boredom, the dilution of a life's value).

6. Fear, living, suicide (22–26) Does fear of death have an object — the state of being dead, or the process of dying? If death is annihilation, is fear of it simply irrational? From there the course turns to living under mortality and to the rationality, uncertainty and morality of suicide, including an examination of the assumption that the value of a life can be weighed.

How to read these notes

One file per lecture, uniform structure: Chapter Overview (timeline navigation) → Overall Summary (condensed through three density-iteration rounds, plus highlights) → Topic Chapters (the lecture's actual order of argument, 2–3 sentences per bullet) → Key Quotes (Kagan's exact words plus context) → Novel Ideas / Counter-intuitive Views / Core Tensions / Methodology / Key Data.

To skim the course: read only the Overall Summary and Key Highlights of each file. To follow the arguments: read Topic Chapters and Core Tensions. To quote the lectures in an essay: take the verbatim English from Key Quotes and locate it in the original video by timestamp.

Source transcripts

The complete English timestamped transcript of every lecture is kept in ../raw/, one file per lecture matching these notes, with the official chapter timeline in its frontmatter. Every Key Quote can be traced back to its point in the original video.
